bull_bear.body:
- **Debt-free** (repaid ₹68.7cr interest-free loan in FY26); ₹403.7cr cash; negative net operating working capital.
- Dividend ₹7/share (70% on FV ₹10) — consistent payout policy driven by operating cash flow.

bull_bear.title: Capital Allocation

bull_bear.body:
- **Central India pricing weakness** persisting 3-4 quarters due to competitor capacity (JK expansion, UltraTech ramp, other new clinker lines); Dalmia/JP-asset 5 MT operationalizing from Q2 adds supply pressure. Mgmt expects parity to follow North India over 1 yr (no "islands of prosperity"); pre-monsoon prices stay soft.
- Fuel/petcoke inflation from West Asia conflict; currency depreciation (importer of fuel).
- Near-full capacity utilization caps volume upside until new capacity lands.
- El Niño/heat-wave → rural demand & food inflation.
- Approval risk: Gujarat EC and MP mine capacity approvals outside company control.
bull_bear.title: Risks

bull_bear.body: Confident and measured. MD repeatedly insists cost push "always gets passed on, with a lag" and that larger players (150/180/100 MT) feel balance-sheet pain more, forcing industry pricing discipline. Bullish on UP election demand. Explicitly cautious / refused "crystal ball gazing" on structural pricing beyond cost-push pass-through, and declined to set timelines for Gujarat plant, MP mines, and Zuari merger. Some Q&A answers vague/evasive on exact numbers (clinker sales volume "difficult to share," blended Kcal cost "need to recheck").
bull_bear.title: Mgmt Tone

bull_bear.body:
- Volume growth (+8.8%) was partly engineered by **lowering clinker factor** (composite cement, −17% clinker) rather than adding clinker — i.e., grinding-side stretch, not capacity addition; gives only "1-2 years" headroom.
- Clinker debottlenecking physically done (3.1→3.23 MT) but **regulatory capacity uplift still pending** — installed vs approved capacity gap.
- Karnataka ~0.5 MT LBTT unit runs at low quantity; total company capacity is ~6.26 MT (not the 5.7-5.75 MT Central India figure analysts quote).
- Parent's 3 MT Karnataka integrated plant sits OUTSIDE the listco — future merger could transfer it in.
- FY EBITDA growth was input-cost-led, NOT price-led (price was a net drag) — margin quality depends on continued fuel optimization.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious

bull_bear.body:
- Part of the Heidelberg Materials Group, leveraging the Group's global sourcing expertise and technology in procurement and operations
- Premium brand build-out: Power Shield, a water-repellent cement, lifted premium-product salience in the trade segment to 13% in FY26 from 10% in FY25, with channel penetration up from 48% in FY25 to 68% in FY26
- Cost structure supported by alternative fuels leadership - Thermal Substitution Rate improved from 1.0% in FY2021-22 to 10.63% in FY2025-26

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Economic and geopolitical risk from India's exposure to global conflicts — Management flags that India is at risk of being drawn into global conflicts; the Middle East North Africa region accounts for USD 225 billion of trade with India and almost 50% of energy supplies as of early 2026, and the fall in the rupee against major currencies compounds the risk. Mitigation is cost reduction, de-bottlenecking, efficiency improvements, new projects and new geographies.
- Fuel and energy input cost volatility — The West Asia conflict has driven fuel prices sharply higher and constrained availability through refinery shutdowns and maritime logistics disruption, causing a sharp escalation in pet coke prices. Diesel and lubricant prices also rose substantially, with limited availability and supply rationing pressuring transporters to seek freight rate revisions. Higher crude, petcoke and coal prices were already visible in Q1 FY27 profitability.
- Raw material supply and import dependence — Imported natural gypsum availability has reduced and prices risen sharply, addressed by increasing domestically sourced chemical gypsum (substitution rate now above 28%). Sweetener procurement of approximately 50 KT per month faces repeated supplier requests for price increases. Packaging is exposed to polymer granule supply constraints and higher costs, since granules are refinery by-products. Uncertainties from the conflict continue to pose potential risks to supply chains and input costs into FY27.
- Competition risk and industry overcapacity — Competition has increased in the Company's core markets, challenging its market share. The industry is witnessing significant capacity additions and competitive intensity, and Indian installed cement capacity of around 720 Mn T against production of around 492 Mn T implies capacity utilisation of only around 70%. Mitigation includes installing a blending and grinding unit at Dongalia, Khandwa, scaling Power Shield and OPC 43, and developing new markets in Rajasthan and Western UP.
- Single-activity and geographic concentration — 100% of turnover comes from a single business activity - manufacturing and selling of cement (NIC 23941) - with markets served in only six states, no international operations and exports of Nil. There is no product or geographic diversification to buffer a downturn in Indian cement or in the Central India core markets.
- Inflation and currency depreciation — The Board's Report flags that ongoing geopolitical developments, particularly the West Asia conflict, create uncertainty in global markets and commodity prices, giving rise to a risk of inflation and currency depreciation. Foreign portfolio investment recorded a net outflow of approximately USD 16.4 billion in FY26, reflecting heightened global risk aversion.
- Weather and rural demand risk — El Nino may pose a potential risk to agricultural output, rural demand and food inflation - a direct exposure for a cement business whose trade channel depends on rural and individual home-building demand.
- Fuel quality inconsistency in domestic sourcing — Although domestic fuel availability improved during the year, quality inconsistencies posed ongoing operational challenges, requiring proactive optimisation of the fuel mix - a structural trade-off of the shift from imported to indigenous fuel.
- Product quality and customer complaints — The BRSR grievance table records 81 customer complaints filed in FY 2025-26 (77 in FY 2024-25) relating to slow setting, low strength and cracks - a recurring product-quality exposure in a brand-driven trade market.

outlook.title: Growth / Optionality

outlook.body:
- Remain disciplined rather than chase growth at any cost: grow volumes while protecting value and pricing discipline in an industry seeing significant capacity additions and rising competitive intensity
- Increase premiumisation of the product mix, led by the Power Shield water-repellent cement brand, targeting salience above 20%
- Continuously reduce cost per tonne through energy efficiency, fuel-mix optimisation, higher alternative fuel consumption, stronger procurement and improved logistics efficiency
- Accelerate energy and sustainability initiatives - non-grid power (solar, wind, Waste Heat Recovery) and alternative fuels - both to cut the environmental footprint and to build resilience against conventional energy price volatility
- Invest selectively in opportunities that strengthen the long-term market position, using the flexibility of a debt-free, cash-rich balance sheet with disciplined capital allocation
- Four-pronged sales strategy under the RISE Sales Excellence Programme: sell more premium products, sell more in high-NSR focus markets, move less and handle less by converting more orders to direct dispatch, and build sales capability
- Digitalisation as an enabler of a simpler, faster and more efficient organisation - technology, automation and data to simplify processes, improve transparency and enhance customer responsiveness
- Expand geographic reach: install a cement blending and grinding unit at Sri Singhaji Thermal Power Plant, Dongalia, Khandwa for western Madhya Pradesh, and develop new markets in Rajasthan and Western Uttar Pradesh
- Raise the share of blended and composite cement, lowering the clinker factor through fly ash, slag and chemical gypsum sourcing arrangements
- Strengthen the channel through the Sambandh+ influencer loyalty programme, Scan2Join influencer capture, and extension of CRM to the non-trade institutional channel
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Expansion in FY26 was incremental and market-driven rather than a large greenfield programme. To counter rising competition in its core markets, the Company is installing a Cement Blending and Grinding Unit at the Sri Singhaji Thermal Power Plant, Dongalia, Khandwa, aimed at market expansion in western Madhya Pradesh, and is developing new markets in Rajasthan and Western Uttar Pradesh. On the resource side, the Company was declared the Preferred Bidder for the grant of two mining leases in Madhya Pradesh, and it entered a long-term fly ash supply agreement with Madhya Pradesh Power Generating Company Limited supported by a dedicated blending unit in Madhya Pradesh; slag supply contracts secure 2 Mn tons per annum for composite cement. Sustainability-linked capex during the year went into a Dust Collector System at the Imlai Cement Grinding Plant and an Alternate Fuels (AFR) project at the Narsingarh clinker plant, which raised alternative fuel consumption in the kilns; capex on such environmental and social technologies was 7.1% of total capex in FY2025-26 versus 7.2% in FY2024-25. Limestone is moved from the Patheria Mines to the Narsingarh clinkerisation plant through a 21-km Overland Belt Conveyor. Product-side expansion included the Power Shield premium water-repellent cement, launched from the Jhansi plant and now also produced at Damoh for central India markets, and the introduction of OPC-43 grade cement for non-trade customers. Green power - solar, wind and Waste Heat Recovery Systems - now meets 43% of electricity requirements, with the share of non-grid power exceeding 50% in FY26. No commissioning dates or rupee project costs were disclosed for the Dongalia grinding unit.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- India's infrastructure push, public capital expenditure, housing, urbanisation and industrial investments provide a solid structural foundation for cement demand; core markets in Central India are well placed to participate
- Management foresees no let-up in cement demand in the construction sector, with FY27 budget provisions - PMAY-Urban, the Urban Challenge Fund, Tier II and III city development, AMRUT and a public capital expenditure increase to Rs 12.2 lakh crore in FY27 - as key drivers
- Cement is expected to follow the last three years' average growth rate of 8%
- Per capita cement consumption in India is steadily increasing but lags the world average of 550 kgs, indicating a large opportunity for infrastructure-led growth
- Indian installed cement capacity was around 720 Mn T in FY26 against production of around 492 Mn T, a capacity utilisation of around 70%, with production growth of 8.7% in FY26
- Lowering GST rates on cement from 28% to 18% is expected to provide an impetus to latent cement demand
- The upcoming Uttar Pradesh election is expected to give impetus to infrastructure spending, housing, rural demand and private construction in Central India
- Near-term outlook is cautiously optimistic but challenging: input costs remain volatile, geopolitical uncertainties persist and competitive intensity within the cement industry is expected to remain high
- Higher crude, petcoke and coal prices, together with increases in logistics and other input costs, are pressuring the industry cost structure; these were already visible in Q1 FY27, where higher input costs hurt profitability despite continued revenue growth
- The industry is witnessing significant capacity additions and competitive intensity, so the Company's focus cannot be on volume growth alone - sustainable value creation requires discipline on pricing, product mix, costs and capital allocation
- Management expects a gradual restoration of normalcy in supply chains during FY27, though the lingering effects of the West Asia conflict continue to pose risks to supply chains and input costs
- Margin levers cited: improved product mix, productivity, cost optimisation and energy efficiency, which drove EBITDA per tonne above Rs 584 per tonne in FY26

thesis: Debt-free, cash-rich (₹403.7cr) Central-India regional cement player running ~90-95% utilization on ~6.26 MT total capacity. FY26 was a beat: volume +8.8%, EBITDA +19.8%, PAT +25.5%, EBITDA/ton up 10% to ₹584. Story now hinges on (a) running into a capacity wall (1-2 yrs of headroom, bought via clinker-factor reduction not new lines), (b) a small ₹130cr Khandwa blending unit (+0.4 MTPA by FY28) as the only near-term hard expansion, and (c) optionality from two newly-won MP limestone mining leases (167 MT reserves) + pending Gujarat EC + eventual Zuari/Karnataka group consolidation. Near-term risk: Central India pricing has been weak 3-4 quarters on competitor capacity additions (JK, UltraTech ramp), and ₹100-160/t fuel cost push in H1FY27 must be passed on with a lag.

- **Volume growth:** In line with Central India industry, which MD expects to grow **7-7.5%** this fiscal (ramping higher into UP elections / early CY). Heidelberg can't fully match industry as it's near full utilization; can sustain ~90% util FY27/FY28 on yearly basis (QoQ harder to predict).
- **EBITDA/ton:** No explicit forward target; FY26 exited at ₹584.
- **Pricing / cost push:** Industry talks of ₹300-400/t H1FY27 cost inflation (fuel + packaging); Heidelberg expects **only ₹100-160/t** impact (₹100-150 next qtr) due to fuel-mix flexibility (shift petcoke→coal). Confident of passing on the cost push "with a lag"; cautious that pre-monsoon pricing stays under "a little bit of pressure."
- **Capex (company-wide):** Sustaining capex ₹45-50cr/yr (~40% of annual depreciation). Khandwa blending unit ₹130cr split over FY27-FY28 (front-light, back-loaded). **Total capex ≈ ₹100cr FY27, ≈ ₹120cr FY28.**
- **Expansion timeline:** Khandwa unit completion within ~2 yrs (CT received). Gujarat plant (2.5-4 MT, not firmed) awaiting govt EC — not in hand. MP mines → "very firm plans," earlier than 4 yrs, no exact date.
demand / pipeline:
- Central India demand outlook strong: monsoon dip then post-monsoon recovery into **UP elections** (highest cement-consuming state) — key demand impetus over next ~1 yr.
- Structural tailwinds: robust domestic consumption; **GST cut 28%→18%** on cement (prior year).
- Headwinds flagged: El Niño / heat wave risk to agri output, rural demand, food inflation (expected mitigated by monsoon); elevated headline inflation + currency depreciation (matters for an importer of fuel).

- ~97% of cement produced is blended (low-carbon); launched composite cement with ~17% lower clinker content, ramping up.
- **Premium products = 52% of trade volumes (+9% YoY)** — 3-yr premiumization strategy.
- Trade mix: **81% trade (retail) / 19% B2B**; ~45% volumes dispatched by road (+1% YoY).

growth / optionality:
- **Khandwa blending unit:** ₹130cr, +30-35k tons/month (~0.4 MTPA), serves a market Damoh can't reach; ~2 yr completion.
- **MP mining leases won (preferred bidder):** Kuria/Shivpur block ~350 ha = 62 MT limestone; second Shivpur block ~350 acres = 105 MT limestone — for "future expansions," details withheld. (167 MT cement-grade reserves total.)

margins & cost:
- FY26 EBITDA/ton ₹584 (+10% YoY); FY price drag −₹16/t offset by RM −₹11/t plus gains in power & fuel, freight, other.
- **Fuel mix flexibility:** petcoke earlier ~60-65%, cut by ~10% over last 2-3 months → coal up from ~30% to ~40%; petcoke now ~30% more expensive than coal on Kcal (petcoke ~₹2-2.25/Kcal vs coal ~₹1.5). Linkage coal sufficient; no open-market purchases of significance.
- **AFR (alt fuel) 11%** (+3% YoY); **non-grid power >50%** of FY; **green power >40%** (target modest increase beyond 40% in FY27/FY28).
- **Lead distance ~370-372 km** (FY26 & Q4 similar; +~5 km over 6 months — not material).

- Khandwa ₹130cr over FY27-FY28 (back-loaded).
- Company-wide ≈ ₹100cr FY27, ≈ ₹120cr FY28.

- Dividend ₹7/share (70% on FV ₹10) — consistent payout policy driven by operating cash flow.

risks:
- **Central India pricing weakness** persisting 3-4 quarters due to competitor capacity (JK expansion, UltraTech ramp, other new clinker lines); Dalmia/JP-asset 5 MT operationalizing from Q2 adds supply pressure. Mgmt expects parity to follow North India over 1 yr (no "islands of prosperity"); pre-monsoon prices stay soft.
- Fuel/petcoke inflation from West Asia conflict; currency depreciation (importer of fuel).
- Near-full capacity utilization caps volume upside until new capacity lands.
- El Niño/heat-wave → rural demand & food inflation.
- Approval risk: Gujarat EC and MP mine capacity approvals outside company control.
mgmt tone: Confident and measured. MD repeatedly insists cost push "always gets passed on, with a lag" and that larger players (150/180/100 MT) feel balance-sheet pain more, forcing industry pricing discipline. Bullish on UP election demand. Explicitly cautious / refused "crystal ball gazing" on structural pricing beyond cost-push pass-through, and declined to set timelines for Gujarat plant, MP mines, and Zuari merger. Some Q&A answers vague/evasive on exact numbers (clinker sales volume "difficult to share," blended Kcal cost "need to recheck").

- Volume growth (+8.8%) was partly engineered by **lowering clinker factor** (composite cement, −17% clinker) rather than adding clinker — i.e., grinding-side stretch, not capacity addition; gives only "1-2 years" headroom.

- Competitor capacity (JK, UltraTech, Dalmia/JP 5 MT) = pricing challenge for incumbents like Heidelberg.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India's infrastructure push, public capital expenditure, housing, urbanisation and industrial investments provide a solid structural foundation for cement demand; core markets in Central India are well placed to participate
- Management foresees no let-up in cement demand in the construction sector, with FY27 budget provisions - PMAY-Urban, the Urban Challenge Fund, Tier II and III city development, AMRUT and a public capital expenditure increase to Rs 12.2 lakh crore in FY27 - as key drivers
- Cement is expected to follow the last three years' average growth rate of 8%
- Per capita cement consumption in India is steadily increasing but lags the world average of 550 kgs, indicating a large opportunity for infrastructure-led growth
- Indian installed cement capacity was around 720 Mn T in FY26 against production of around 492 Mn T, a capacity utilisation of around 70%, with production growth of 8.7% in FY26
- Lowering GST rates on cement from 28% to 18% is expected to provide an impetus to latent cement demand
- The upcoming Uttar Pradesh election is expected to give impetus to infrastructure spending, housing, rural demand and private construction in Central India
- Near-term outlook is cautiously optimistic but challenging: input costs remain volatile, geopolitical uncertainties persist and competitive intensity within the cement industry is expected to remain high
- Higher crude, petcoke and coal prices, together with increases in logistics and other input costs, are pressuring the industry cost structure; these were already visible in Q1 FY27, where higher input costs hurt profitability despite continued revenue growth
- The industry is witnessing significant capacity additions and competitive intensity, so the Company's focus cannot be on volume growth alone - sustainable value creation requires discipline on pricing, product mix, costs and capital allocation
- Management expects a gradual restoration of normalcy in supply chains during FY27, though the lingering effects of the West Asia conflict continue to pose risks to supply chains and input costs
- Margin levers cited: improved product mix, productivity, cost optimisation and energy efficiency, which drove EBITDA per tonne above Rs 584 per tonne in FY26

- **AFR (alt fuel) 11%** (+3% YoY); **non-grid power >50%** of FY; **green power >40%** (target modest increase beyond 40% in FY27/FY28).

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Expansion in FY26 was incremental and market-driven rather than a large greenfield programme. To counter rising competition in its core markets, the Company is installing a Cement Blending and Grinding Unit at the Sri Singhaji Thermal Power Plant, Dongalia, Khandwa, aimed at market expansion in western Madhya Pradesh, and is developing new markets in Rajasthan and Western Uttar Pradesh. On the resource side, the Company was declared the Preferred Bidder for the grant of two mining leases in Madhya Pradesh, and it entered a long-term fly ash supply agreement with Madhya Pradesh Power Generating Company Limited supported by a dedicated blending unit in Madhya Pradesh; slag supply contracts secure 2 Mn tons per annum for composite cement. Sustainability-linked capex during the year went into a Dust Collector System at the Imlai Cement Grinding Plant and an Alternate Fuels (AFR) project at the Narsingarh clinker plant, which raised alternative fuel consumption in the kilns; capex on such environmental and social technologies was 7.1% of total capex in FY2025-26 versus 7.2% in FY2024-25. Limestone is moved from the Patheria Mines to the Narsingarh clinkerisation plant through a 21-km Overland Belt Conveyor. Product-side expansion included the Power Shield premium water-repellent cement, launched from the Jhansi plant and now also produced at Damoh for central India markets, and the introduction of OPC-43 grade cement for non-trade customers. Green power - solar, wind and Waste Heat Recovery Systems - now meets 43% of electricity requirements, with the share of non-grid power exceeding 50% in FY26. No commissioning dates or rupee project costs were disclosed for the Dongalia grinding unit.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:

- Premium brand build-out: Power Shield, a water-repellent cement, lifted premium-product salience in the trade segment to 13% in FY26 from 10% in FY25, with channel penetration up from 48% in FY25 to 68% in FY26

themes.title: Cement demand & pricing recovery
themes.need: Q1FY27 turned cement from a pricing story into a volume-share-plus-fuel-cost story. ULTRACEMCO grew domestic grey volume +13.1% YoY against an estimated ~7-8% industry, delivered its first Rs 5,000cr+ April-June EBITDA (Rs 5,146cr) with EBITDA/ton held above Rs 1,200, and crossed 200.1 MT domestic capacity a year early - but guided Q2FY27 cost UP ~Rs 130-140/ton and pinned the Rs 1,400/ton consolidated target to Q4FY28. The fuel shock, not price, is the swing factor: JKCEMENT's EBITDA/ton fell to Rs 982 from Rs 1,229 YoY despite +19% grey volume, DALBHARAT flagged pet coke 'surged to nearly $160/t' versus a pre-war $110-115, and NUVOCO defended INR 1,079/ton EBITDA only by cutting petcoke from 37% to 27% of fuel mix in a single quarter. Consolidation is visibly compounding (INDIACEM EBITDA/ton Rs 386->400->509->603 across four quarters; DALBHARAT closed Jaypee at Rs 2,850cr EV with Chunar operational and Rewa on trial within 50 days) even as DALBHARAT slipped its 75mt milestone from FY27 to FY28. SHREECEM/RAMCOCEM/JKLAKSHMI/JSWCEMENT/STARCEMENT/BIRLACORPN ride the same volume + consolidation axis.
themes.driver: Q2FY27 is the guided cost trough - ULTRACEMCO ~Rs 130-140/ton, JKCEMENT ~Rs 150/ton and BIRLACORPN Rs 70-80/ton of incremental cost; then fuel-mix agility (NUVOCO's petcoke swing) and whether DALBHARAT's ~Rs 150/t of procurement savings is really 'permanent, not timing'.
